On such occasions poor Mr. Woodhouse found his feelings in a melancholy conflict. He liked the cloth to be laid, for it had been the fashion of his youth, yet his conviction that heavy suppers were very unwholesome made him rather uneasy at seeing anything placed upon it; and while his hospitality would have welcomed his visitors to everything, his concern for their health caused him sorrow at the thought of them eating.

A small basin of thin gruel, like his own, was all he could, with thorough self‑approval, recommend; though he might restrain himself, while the ladies were comfortably clearing away the finer dishes, to say:

“Mrs. Bates, may I suggest you try one of these eggs? A very soft‑boiled egg is not unwholesome. Serle knows how to boil an egg better than anyone. I would not recommend an egg boiled by anyone else; but you need not be frightened, they are very small, you see—one of our little eggs will not hurt you. Miss Bates, let Emma give you a _little_ bit of tart—a _very_ little bit. Ours are all apple‑tarts. You need not fear unwholesome preserves here. I do not advise the custard. Mrs. Goddard, what say you to _half_ a glass of wine? A _small_ half‑glass, diluted with water? I do not think it could disagree with you.”

Emma permitted her father to speak—but she served her guests in a far more satisfactory manner, and on that particular evening took particular pleasure in seeing them depart contented. The happiness of Miss Smith matched her intentions exactly. Miss Woodhouse was such a great figure in Highbury that the prospect of the introduction had brought both anxiety and delight; yet the modest, grateful little girl left with a highly gratified spirit, delighted by the kindness with which Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening, and at last even shook her hand!

She had been badly afflicted by cramp after dancing, and her first attempt to climb the bank provoked such a violent recurrence that she was utterly powerless, left in a state of extreme fright and forced to stay where she was.

What the ruffians might have done if the young ladies had shown more bravery is uncertain, but such an invitation to attack could not be ignored. At that moment Frank Churchill happened upon her, trembling and disordered, while the children were loud and insolent. She added more strongly, "I am comforted now that it was only a mistake of imagination on my part, and that it has hurt no one but myself."

"My dear Jane," Elizabeth exclaimed, "you are too good. Your kindness and selflessness are almost angelic; I don’t know what to say. I feel I have never treated you fairly or loved you as you deserve."

Jane quickly denied any special merit and returned the praise to her sister’s warm affection.

"No," said Elizabeth, "that isn’t fair. You want to think everyone is respectable and get hurt if I say anything bad about anyone. I only want to think of you as perfect, and you push back against that. Don’t worry that I will go too far or take away your right to be liked by everyone."

It was Mr. Collins’s description of Hunsford and Rosings that had become, at last, reasonably softened; and Elizabeth realized that she would have to wait for her own journey there before she could learn the rest.

Jane had already sent a short note to her sister, announcing their safe arrival in London; and when she wrote again, Elizabeth hoped she would be able to say something about the Bingleys.

Her eagerness for this second letter was rewarded, as impatience often is. Jane had spent a week in the city without either seeing or hearing from Caroline. She explained it by supposing that her last letter to her friend at Longbourn had somehow been lost.

“My aunt,” she continued, “is going tomorrow into that part of town, and I shall take the opportunity of calling in Grosvenor Street.”

She wrote again after the visit was made, and after she had seen Miss Bingley. “I did not think Caroline in spirits,” she wrote, “but she was very glad to see me, and reproached me for giving her no notice of my coming to London. I found that Miss Darcy was expected to dinner: I wish I could see her. My visit was not long, as Caroline and Mrs. Hurst were going out. I dare say I shall soon see them here.”

Elizabeth shook her head over this letter. It convinced her that only an accident could have revealed to Mr. Bingley her sister’s presence in town.

Four weeks passed, and Jane saw nothing of him. She tried to convince herself that she did not regret it; but she could no longer ignore Miss Bingley’s indifference. After waiting at home each morning for a fortnight, and inventing a fresh excuse each evening for her, the visitor finally appeared; yet the brevity of her stay, and especially the change in her manner, left Jane unable to deceive herself any longer. The letter she wrote on that occasion to her sister shows what she felt:

“My dearest Lizzy, I am sure you will be unable to triumph in your better judgment at my expense when I confess that I have been completely misled by Miss Bingley’s regard for me. I do not at all understand her reason for wishing to be intimate with me; but, if the same circumstances were to happen again, I am sure I would be deceived again. Caroline did not return my visit until yesterday; and not a note, not a line, did I receive in the meantime. Elizabeth was ready to see him at his best; she could not help imagining that by showing off the room's good proportions, its view, and its furnishings, he was directing his attention especially toward her, as if trying to make her sense what she missed by refusing him. Yet, although everything appeared tidy and pleasant, she could not offer him any sigh of regret; instead she stared in amazement at her friend, wondering how she could maintain such a cheerful demeanor with such a companion. Whenever Mr. Collins said something that might reasonably embarrass his wife—a frequent occurrence—Elizabeth involuntarily glanced at Charlotte. Occasionally she caught a faint blush, but generally Charlotte seemed to hear nothing.

After they had sat long enough to inspect every piece of furniture, from the sideboard to the fender, and after Mr. Collins recounted their journey and the events in London, he suggested they walk in the garden, which was spacious and well arranged, and which he tended himself. Working in his garden was one of his most respectable pleasures; Elizabeth admired the confident manner in which Charlotte spoke of the health benefits of the exercise, and she confessed she encouraged it as much as she could.

Leading them along every path and crossing, allowing them scarcely a moment to utter the praises he demanded, he described each view with such meticulous detail that the beauty was almost lost. He could count the fields in every direction and tell exactly how many trees stood in the farthest clump. Yet, of all the scenes his garden, the countryside, or the kingdom could offer, none compared with the prospect of Rosings, visible through an opening in the trees that bordered the park almost directly opposite his house. It was a handsome, modern building set on rising ground.

From his garden Mr. Collins intended to show them his two meadows, but the ladies, lacking shoes suitable for the lingering frost, turned back; while Sir William walked with him, Charlotte escorted her sister and friend around the house, evidently delighted to have the chance to display it without her husband's assistance. The house was modest but well constructed and convenient; everything was arranged with a neatness and uniformity for which Elizabeth gave Charlotte full credit. When Mr. Collins faded from attention, a genuine sense of comfort pervaded, and from Charlotte’s obvious enjoyment, Elizabeth guessed that he was often forgotten.
